w: Three working radio telescopes and a museum named for Grote Reber - the amateur engineer who built the world's first parabolic radio telescope in his own backyard - sit twenty kilometres east of the city. Run by the University of Tasmania, it is still listening to the sky.
s: A museum for the man who invented the radio telescope.
_facts: Radio-astronomy observatory owned and operated by the University of Tasmania, 20km east of Hobart in Cambridge
Home to three radio astronomy antennas and the Grote Reber Museum

w: Fourteen hectares tucked into the Queens Domain, a quiet public garden rather than a tourist set piece. It has grown steadily since its founding, still doing what a colonial-era botanical garden was built to do: hold a living collection and let people wander through it.
s: Fourteen quiet hectares on the Queens Domain.
_facts: Public botanical garden covering approximately 14 hectares, in Hobart within the Queens Domain

w: The cathedral's story starts in 1822 with a temporary wooden chapel, built by the first permanent priest ever stationed in Tasmania and dedicated to St Virgilius - an obscure Irish saint for a very new colony. It has been the seat of Hobart's Catholic archbishops ever since.
s: A convict-era chapel that grew into a cathedral.
_facts: Seat of the Roman Catholic Archbishop of Hobart
Origins trace to 1822, when the first permanent Tasmanian priest, Philip Conolly, built a temporary wooden chapel near the present site
That chapel was dedicated to St Virgilius, described as 'an Irish Saint'

w: Launched as a Royal Navy minesweeper, HMS Chediston, before crossing to Australia under a new name - Curlew patrolled off Malaysia through the Indonesia-Malaysia confrontation, then soldiered on as a minehunter years past her intended retirement before finally being sold off in 1991.
s: A Cold War minesweeper's very long retirement.
_facts: Ton-class minesweeper, operated by the Royal Navy as HMS Chediston 1953-1961, then the Royal Australian Navy 1962-1991
Operated off Malaysia during the Indonesia-Malaysia confrontation in the mid-1960s, later modified as a minehunter
Kept operational until 1990 by delays in a replacement class; sold into civilian service in 1991

w: One roof for the reference collection, the reading room, the state's archives and its heritage records - Libraries Tasmania runs the lot from here. Less a single building than the switchboard for how the whole island keeps its paper trail and its literacy programs running.
s: The switchboard for Tasmania's paper trail.
_facts: Reference, special collections, research and public lending library in Hobart, part of Libraries Tasmania
Libraries Tasmania also runs state-wide library services, community learning, adult literacy, and the state's archives and heritage services

w: This was Hobart's first burial ground, and the city's founding Lieutenant Governor, David Collins, is still down there under the English landscape garden that replaced the headstones. The memorial walls keep the names; the roses and lawns keep visitors from noticing it's a cemetery.
s: A founder's grave under an English garden.
_facts: Heritage-listed park bounded by Davey Street, Salamanca Place and Sandy Bay Road
Originally served as Hobart's primary burial ground, final resting place of early settlers including founding Lieutenant Governor David Collins
Now an English landscape garden with memorial walls and historical monuments

w: Female convicts served their sentences behind these walls from 1828 to 1856, in just three surviving yards from an original five. Now part of the UNESCO-listed Australian Convict Sites, it is the clearest surviving record of what transportation actually meant for women in Van Diemen's Land.
s: Where Van Diemen's Land held its female convicts.
_facts: Former workhouse for female convicts in the penal colony of Van Diemen's Land, South Hobart, operational 1828-1856
One of 11 sites forming the Australian Convict Sites, UNESCO World Heritage listed
Consists of three of the original five yards; now a museum, open daily except Christmas

n: Museum of Old and New Art
w: David Walsh built the largest privately funded museum in the Southern Hemisphere into a winery peninsula and filled it with a collection obsessed with sex and death - his own words call it 'a subversive adult Disneyland.' Since 2011 it has spun off Dark Mofo and Mona Foma, Hobart's wildest festivals.
s: A subversive adult Disneyland, in Walsh's own words.
_facts: Art museum within the Moorilla winery on the Berriedale peninsula, Hobart
Largest privately funded museum in the Southern Hemisphere, houses the David Walsh collection, themed around sex and death
Walsh described it as 'a subversive adult Disneyland'; officially opened 21 January 2011
Hosts the annual Mona Foma and Dark Mofo music and arts festivals

w: Built in 1845 in full Egyptian Revival regalia - lotus-capital columns, trapezoidal windows - on land that once belonged to a former convict. The back rows still hold the hard benches installed for Jewish convicts marched in under guard: reputedly the only synagogue anywhere built with seats for prisoners.
s: The only synagogue built with seats for convicts.
_facts: Heritage-listed, at 59 Argyle Street; oldest synagogue building in Australia, rare Egyptian Revival style, built 1845
Land previously part of the garden of former convict Judah Solomon
Seats 150, with hard benches at the back installed for Jewish convicts marched in under armed guard
Believed to be the only synagogue in the world with seats set aside for convicts

w: Sweeping gardens with commanding Derwent views once housed a zoo here, right by the Governor's residence and the Botanical Gardens - now mostly swallowed by a council depot. Look hard enough among the sheds and you can still find fragments of the old enclosures, left where the animals were.
s: A vanished zoo, hiding behind a council depot.
_facts: Also known as Beaumaris Zoo, an old-fashioned zoological garden on the Queen's Domain, Hobart
Very close to the site of the Tasmanian Governor's House and the Botanical Gardens
Site now primarily a Hobart City Council depot, though some remnants and archaeological remains of the zoo survive
Set in sweeping gardens with commanding views across the River Derwent

w: Noel Coward called it 'a dream of a theatre'; Laurence Olivier thought it worth saving enough to launch a national appeal for its reconstruction in the 1940s. Both were right to fuss - it remains the oldest continually operating theatre in Australia, curtain up night after night.
s: Australia's oldest theatre, saved by Olivier's appeal.
_facts: Historic performing arts venue in central Hobart, oldest continually operating theatre in Australia
Noel Coward called it 'a dream of a theatre'
Laurence Olivier launched a national appeal for its reconstruction in the 1940s

w: Dolerite peaks scoured by old glaciers form the backbone behind Hobart, topped by kunanyi/Mount Wellington at 1,269 metres. Collins Cap, Collins Bonnet, Trestle Mountain and half a dozen more summits hide behind that famous one, all folded into the one park reserve.
_facts: Mountain range in south-east Tasmania, mainly dolerite, showing evidence of past glaciation
Includes kunanyi/Mount Wellington at 1,269 metres, plus Collins Cap, Collins Bonnet, Trestle Mountain, Mount Marian, Mount Charles and Mount Patrick
Part of the Wellington Park Reserve

w: The exhibits sit inside an 1847 military jail that later did time as a girls' reformatory, married quarters and a store before anyone thought to make it a museum. It now tracks Tasmania's soldiers from the British colonial garrison at Anglesea Barracks through to current deployments.
s: A colonial jail that became a war museum.
_facts: Formerly the Military Museum of Tasmania, within Anglesea Barracks, Hobart, constructed 1814, on the Commonwealth Heritage List
Museum housed in the military jail built 1847, which also served as a girls' reformatory, married quarters, and a store over the years
Displays span the colonial period through to current Australian Defence Force deployments, with a focus on Tasmanian servicemen and women

w: Built to take advantage of one of the best southern-sky views around - close enough to the pole to watch the Magellanic Clouds - this university observatory eventually lost the fight against its own city. Hobart's suburban lights crept close enough that the sky simply stopped cooperating, and it closed.
s: An observatory the city's own lights shut down.
_facts: Optical astronomy observatory belonging to the University of Tasmania, about 12km from Hobart
High southern latitude allowed observation of the Magellanic Clouds
Closed due to encroaching light pollution from Hobart's suburbs
